question: What does @RestController do in Spring Boot?
title: @RestController in Spring Boot — Annotation Explained
direct_answer: **`@RestController`** is a composed annotation that combines `@Controller` and `@ResponseBody`. It marks a class as a Spring-managed controller where every method automatically serializes its return value to the HTTP response body (JSON by default with Jackson).

interviewer_intent.testing: Core annotation knowledge — used in every REST API
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @RestController makes @ResponseBody implicit — adding @ResponseBody explicitly is redundant
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @RestController is a 'meta-annotation' composed of @Controller + @ResponseBody

sections.title: @RestController Explained
@RestController Key Points
sections.content:
- **Composed annotation**: `@RestController` = `@Controller + @ResponseBody`
- **JSON default**: With Jackson on classpath, return objects are serialized to JSON automatically
- **No view resolution**: Return values go to MessageConverter, not ViewResolver
- **Spring bean**: `@Controller` part means it's auto-detected by component scanning
- **Base path**: Pair with `@RequestMapping("/api/resource")` at class level for URL prefix
- **HTTP status**: Returns 200 OK by default; use `ResponseEntity` for custom status codes
- **@ResponseBody NOT needed**: Adding it explicitly on methods inside @RestController is redundant
- **Per-method override**: `@Controller` class method can return JSON with `@ResponseBody` — same as if in @RestController

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @RestController is a shortcut composed of two annotations: @Controller, which registers the class as a Spring bean discoverable by component scanning, and @ResponseBody, which tells Spring to serialize every method's return value directly into the HTTP response body. Before @RestController existed in Spring 4, you had to put @ResponseBody on every method individually — @RestController eliminated that boilerplate. With Jackson on the classpath, every method's return value is automatically converted to JSON. The default HTTP status code is 200 OK. If you need to return a different status code or add custom headers, you'd return a ResponseEntity object instead of a plain return type.

What HTTP status code does @RestController return by default?
How do you return a custom HTTP status code from a @RestController method?

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @RestController is a composed annotation that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody. @Controller registers the class as a Spring bean picked up by component scanning. @ResponseBody tells Spring to serialize every method's return value directly into the HTTP response body instead of treating it as a view name.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Before Spring 4, you had to add @ResponseBody to every single method in a REST controller. @RestController was introduced to eliminate that repetition. One annotation on the class, and all methods get the behavior.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: Default HTTP status: 200 OK for every method unless you override it.
JSON output: with Jackson on the classpath, return objects are serialized to JSON automatically.
No view resolution: return values go to MessageConverter, not ViewResolver.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: @RestController already includes @ResponseBody. Adding @ResponseBody explicitly on methods inside a @RestController class is redundant — it does nothing extra. Interviewers notice that.

speakable_v2.cap: Use ResponseEntity when you need custom headers or conditional status codes. For everything else, a plain return type with @RestController is cleaner.

question: What is the difference between @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, and @PatchMapping?
title: HTTP Method Annotations in Spring — GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH
direct_answer: Each annotation maps a controller method to a specific HTTP verb: `@GetMapping` for reads, `@PostMapping` for creates, `@PutMapping` for full updates, `@DeleteMapping` for deletes, `@PatchMapping` for partial updates. All are shorthand for `@RequestMapping(method=RequestMethod.X)`.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @PostMapping for updates — should use @PutMapping (full replace) or @PatchMapping (partial)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain idempotency: GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST is not

sections.title: HTTP Method Annotations
HTTP Method Semantics
sections.content:
- **`@GetMapping`**: Read operation — safe and idempotent — no request body
- **`@PostMapping`**: Create new resource — NOT idempotent (multiple calls = multiple creates)
- **`@PutMapping`**: Full update/replace — idempotent — send complete entity
- **`@PatchMapping`**: Partial update — send only changed fields (not idempotent in practice)
- **`@DeleteMapping`**: Delete resource — idempotent
- **Idempotency**: Same request gives same result — GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST is not
- **Status codes**: POST → 201 Created; GET → 200 OK; PUT/PATCH → 200 or 204 No Content; DELETE → 204 No Content
- **Request body**: @GetMapping/@DeleteMapping don't have request bodies; @PostMapping/@PutMapping/@PatchMapping do

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: These are the five main HTTP method annotations in Spring REST. @GetMapping is for reading data — it's safe and idempotent, no request body. @PostMapping creates a new resource — it's NOT idempotent, meaning calling it multiple times creates multiple records. @PutMapping is for full updates — you send the complete representation of the resource, replacing the existing one — it IS idempotent. @PatchMapping is for partial updates — only send what changed. @DeleteMapping removes a resource. A key interview point about idempotency: GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent — calling them multiple times has the same effect. POST is not idempotent. For REST API response codes: POST should return 201 Created, DELETE and PUT should return 204 No Content when there's nothing to return.

followup_questions: What is idempotency and which HTTP methods are idempotent?
What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
What HTTP status code should a POST request return on success?

seo.metaDescription: Learn Spring HTTP method annotations — GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE semantics, idempotency, and correct response status codes for REST APIs.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: Five HTTP methods, five annotations — but the real question is which one matches the operation you're actually performing.

beats.label: optimising_for
beats.content: Each mapping annotation corresponds to an HTTP verb with a specific semantic meaning in REST. Picking the right one isn't just style — it signals intent to every developer and every HTTP client that sees your API.

beats.label: options
rows: Full replace — send the whole entity
Partial update — send only changed fields

beats.label: tradeoffs
beats.content: Idempotency is the key concept here. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent — calling them ten times has the same effect as calling them once. POST is not — ten POST calls create ten records. PATCH is technically not idempotent in the general case either.

beats.label: decision
beats.content: Use @PostMapping and return 201 Created for creates. Use @DeleteMapping and return 204 No Content when there's nothing to return. Use @PutMapping when the client sends a full replacement. Use @PatchMapping when they send only what changed.

beats.label: rethink_if
beats.content: sharp edge: Using @PostMapping for updates is a common fresher mistake. A POST that creates ten identical resources is correct REST. If you only want one resource to exist, you need PUT or PATCH.

speakable_v2.cap: All five annotations are shorthand for @RequestMapping with the method pre-set. You can always fall back to @RequestMapping if you need to match multiple HTTP methods.
followup_handoff: What is idempotency and which HTTP methods are idempotent?

question: How does Jackson serialize Java objects to JSON in Spring Boot?
title: Jackson JSON Serialization in Spring Boot — Auto-Configuration
direct_answer: Spring Boot auto-configures **Jackson's `ObjectMapper`** as the default JSON serializer. When a `@RestController` method returns a Java object, Spring's `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter` calls `ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString(object)` and writes the result to the HTTP response body.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JSON serialization mechanics in Spring Boot
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Jackson uses getter names by default — a field without a getter won't be serialized

sections.title: Jackson Serialization Flow
sections.content:
```
@RestController method returns User { id: 1, name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com" }
    ↓
MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter
    ↓
Jackson ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString(user)
    ↓
{"id":1,"name":"Alice","email":"alice@example.com"}
    ↓
HTTP Response body with Content-Type: application/json
```

sections.title: Jackson Configuration and Annotations
sections.content:
- **Serialization**: Java → JSON (response body)
- **Deserialization**: JSON → Java (`@RequestBody`)
- **Default behavior**: Jackson serializes all public fields and getter return values
- **`@JsonIgnore`**: Exclude field from JSON (e.g., don't serialize `password`)
- **`@JsonProperty("user_name")`**: Override JSON field name (camelCase Java → snake_case JSON)
- **`@JsonInclude(JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL)`**: Exclude null fields from JSON output
- **`@JsonFormat(pattern="yyyy-MM-dd")`**: Format dates in JSON
- **`application.properties`**: `spring.jackson.serialization.indent-output=true` for pretty-print
- **Custom ObjectMapper**: `@Bean ObjectMapper objectMapper()` to override Spring Boot's defaults
- **Circular reference**: `@JsonManagedReference` / `@JsonBackReference` to handle bidirectional relationships

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Jackson is Spring Boot's default JSON library, auto-configured when you add spring-boot-starter-web. When your @RestController method returns a Java object, Spring passes it to MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, which uses Jackson's ObjectMapper to convert it to a JSON string. By default, Jackson serializes all fields with getters. You can customize this behavior with Jackson annotations: @JsonIgnore to exclude sensitive fields like passwords, @JsonProperty to rename fields in JSON, @JsonInclude to skip null fields, @JsonFormat for date formatting. If you need global Jackson settings, you can define an ObjectMapper bean in your configuration class and Spring Boot will use it instead of the default.

followup_questions: How do you exclude a field from JSON serialization in Spring Boot?
What is @JsonProperty and when do you use it?
How do you handle circular references in JSON serialization?

seo.metaTitle: Jackson JSON Serialization in Spring Boot | Interview Guide
seo.metaDescription: Learn how Jackson serializes Java objects to JSON in Spring Boot — ObjectMapper, MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, @JsonIgnore, @JsonProperty explained.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: Jackson is what actually turns your Java objects into JSON — and knowing how it works helps you fix serialization bugs fast.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: Jackson is Spring Boot's default JSON library. When your @RestController method returns a Java object, Spring passes it to MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, which uses Jackson's ObjectMapper to convert it to JSON. Spring Boot auto-configures all of this when spring-boot-starter-web is on your classpath.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: By default, Jackson serializes fields that have public getters. If a field has no getter, it won't appear in the JSON output. This is why Lombok's @Getter or manually writing getters is important for DTO classes.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: @JsonIgnore: exclude a field entirely — typical use is hiding password fields.
@JsonProperty("user_name"): rename the field in the JSON output.
@JsonInclude(NON_NULL): skip fields that are null, keeping the JSON clean.
@JsonFormat(pattern="yyyy-MM-dd"): control how dates appear in JSON.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: production trap: Bidirectional JPA relationships like User has many Orders, Order has a User cause infinite recursion during serialization. Jackson follows each reference back and forth until a stack overflow. Use @JsonManagedReference and @JsonBackReference, or better yet, use DTOs instead of serializing entities directly.

speakable_v2.cap: Define an ObjectMapper bean in your configuration class to set global Jackson behavior — things like date format, null handling, or pretty printing.

question: What is @ResponseStatus in Spring MVC?
title: @ResponseStatus in Spring — Custom HTTP Status Codes
direct_answer: **`@ResponseStatus`** sets the HTTP status code for a controller method's response or marks an exception class with the status code that should be returned when that exception is thrown. It's a cleaner alternative to returning `ResponseEntity` when you just need to set the status code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of HTTP status code control in Spring REST
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @ResponseStatus exists — using ResponseEntity for everything when @ResponseStatus is cleaner
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show @ResponseStatus on exception class to auto-map exception to HTTP status

sections.title: @ResponseStatus Usage
@ResponseStatus Notes
sections.content:
- **On method**: Sets HTTP status for successful response (e.g., 201 for POST, 204 for DELETE with no content)
- **On exception class**: Maps that exception type to a specific HTTP status — no need for @ExceptionHandler
- **`reason` attribute**: Sets response body to this message (but Spring may wrap it in error structure)
- **vs ResponseEntity**: @ResponseStatus is simpler when you only need status, not custom headers or body control
- **`@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)`**: For DELETE/PUT endpoints that return nothing
- **`@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)`**: Correct status for POST endpoints
- **Limitation**: Can't change status dynamically based on logic — use `ResponseEntity` for conditional status codes
- **@ControllerAdvice**: More powerful exception handling than @ResponseStatus on exception class

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @ResponseStatus is used to declare what HTTP status code a controller method or exception should produce. On a method, it's a clean way to say 'this POST endpoint should return 201 Created' without wrapping the return in a ResponseEntity. You just annotate the method and return your object normally. On an exception class, it's a simple way to map that exception type to an HTTP status — if you annotate UserNotFoundException with @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND), any time that exception propagates out of a controller, Spring automatically returns a 404 without you writing an @ExceptionHandler. For more complex scenarios — custom error response body, conditional status codes — you'd use ResponseEntity or @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @ResponseStatus and ResponseEntity?
How do you return 201 Created from a POST endpoint?
When would you use @ResponseStatus on an exception class vs @ExceptionHandler?

seo.metaTitle: @ResponseStatus in Spring MVC | Java Fresher Interview Guide
seo.metaDescription: Learn @ResponseStatus in Spring MVC — setting HTTP status codes on methods and exception classes, 201 Created, 204 No Content, difference from ResponseEntity.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: @ResponseStatus is the simple path to custom HTTP status codes — ResponseEntity is the powerful one. Pick based on what you need.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: @ResponseStatus is an annotation you put on a method or an exception class to declare what HTTP status code it produces. It's declarative and static — you set it once and it always applies.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: ResponseEntity is a return type that gives you full programmatic control — status code, headers, and body all in one object. You build it in the method body, so the status can depend on runtime logic.

beats.label: differences
content: @ResponseStatus on a method: always returns that status code, no conditions.
@ResponseStatus on an exception class: any time that exception propagates out of a controller, Spring returns that status automatically — no @ExceptionHandler needed.
ResponseEntity: build the response programmatically — status, headers, and body all customizable at runtime.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: Use @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) on a simple POST method when you always return 201. Use ResponseEntity when you need to conditionally return 200 or 404, or add Location headers. Use @ResponseStatus on a custom exception class as a simple mapping without writing an @ExceptionHandler.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: non-obvious: @ResponseStatus has a reason attribute that sets the response body message. But Spring wraps it in the standard error response format — you don't get full control over the body. For a custom error body shape, use @ExceptionHandler with ResponseEntity.

speakable_v2.cap: For basic status code control, @ResponseStatus is cleaner. For any runtime logic, custom headers, or precise error body shape, use ResponseEntity.

question: What is @CrossOrigin in Spring Boot and what does CORS mean?
title: @CrossOrigin in Spring Boot — CORS Configuration for REST APIs
direct_answer: **CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)** is a browser security policy that blocks JavaScript from calling APIs on a different domain. **`@CrossOrigin`** in Spring enables CORS for specific controllers/methods by adding the necessary response headers, allowing browsers from specified origins to make API calls.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of the CORS problem every REST API developer faces
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Disabling CORS entirely with allowedOrigins('*') — security risk in production
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain global CORS config via WebMvcConfigurer as cleaner alternative to @CrossOrigin on every controller

sections.title: CORS and @CrossOrigin
CORS Configuration Options
sections.content:
- **`@CrossOrigin(origins='http://frontend.com')`**: Enable CORS for specific controller/method
- **`@CrossOrigin(origins='*')`**: Allow all origins — OK for dev, not for production
- **Global config**: `WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings()` — configure once for all endpoints
- **CORS headers added**: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, etc.
- **Preflight request**: Browser sends OPTIONS request before POST/PUT to check CORS policy
- **`allowCredentials=true`**: Required for cookies/auth tokens — cannot use `origins='*'` with this
- **Spring Security + CORS**: If you have Spring Security, CORS config must also be set there (`.cors()` in SecurityFilterChain)
- **`allowedHeaders`**: Specify which request headers are allowed

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, and it's a browser security mechanism that prevents JavaScript on one domain from calling APIs on a different domain. The classic scenario in Spring Boot is a React frontend on port 3000 trying to call a backend API on port 8080 — the browser blocks this as a cross-origin request. @CrossOrigin on your controller tells Spring to add the appropriate CORS response headers so the browser allows the request. For production, you'd configure CORS globally using WebMvcConfigurer's addCorsMappings method, specifying exactly which origins are allowed rather than using wildcard star. If you're also using Spring Security, you need to configure CORS there too — Spring Security processes requests before Spring MVC, so it can block preflight OPTIONS requests before they reach your CORS configuration.

followup_questions: What is a CORS preflight request?
Why can't you use allowedOrigins('*') with allowCredentials(true)?
How do you configure CORS globally in Spring Boot?

seo.metaTitle: @CrossOrigin and CORS in Spring Boot | Java Fresher Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn CORS and @CrossOrigin in Spring Boot — what CORS is, @CrossOrigin annotation, global WebMvcConfigurer CORS config, and Spring Security CORS.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: CORS errors in the browser are one of the most common shocks when you first connect a React frontend to a Spring Boot API.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. It's a browser security policy that blocks JavaScript on one origin from calling an API on a different origin. An origin is the combination of protocol, domain, and port — so localhost:3000 and localhost:8080 are different origins even though they're on the same machine.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: The browser enforces CORS to prevent malicious sites from making authenticated API calls on your behalf. It's not a Spring limitation — it's enforced by every browser. The server has to explicitly opt in to cross-origin requests by sending CORS response headers.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: @CrossOrigin on a controller: adds CORS headers for all methods in that class.
WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings: global CORS config applied to all endpoints — the cleaner production approach.
Preflight request: before a POST or PUT, the browser sends an OPTIONS request to check if cross-origin is allowed. Spring handles this automatically.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: sharp edge: allowedOrigins('*') allows every domain and is fine in development. But you can't combine it with allowCredentials(true) — that combination is rejected by the browser's CORS spec. In production, list your specific frontend domains explicitly.

speakable_v2.cap: If you add Spring Security later, configure CORS there too — Security processes requests before Spring MVC and can block preflight OPTIONS requests before your CORS config runs.

question: What is @RequestMapping at class level vs method level in Spring?
title: @RequestMapping at Class vs Method Level — URL Composition
direct_answer: **Class-level `@RequestMapping`** sets the base URL prefix for all methods in the class. **Method-level** annotations (`@GetMapping`, etc.) add sub-paths to the base. Spring combines them: class `/api/users` + method `/{id}` = full URL `/api/users/{id}`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring MVC URL structuring knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Duplicating the base path in every method mapping instead of using class-level @RequestMapping
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how class-level and method-level paths combine and mention @RequestMapping can hold multiple paths

sections.title: URL Composition with @RequestMapping
Class vs Method Level Mapping
sections.content:
- **Class-level `@RequestMapping`**: Sets base URL — avoids repeating it in every method
- **Method-level**: Relative to class-level base; if no class-level, method path is absolute
- **Path concatenation**: Class `/api/users` + Method `/{id}` = `/api/users/{id}` (Spring handles the `/` joining)
- **No class-level**: Method path is the full path from root
- **Multiple paths**: `@RequestMapping({"/users", "/people"})` — array of paths
- **API versioning**: Use class-level path for version: `/api/v1/users` vs `/api/v2/users`
- **HTTP method on class**: Class-level @RequestMapping(method=GET) restricts all methods to GET — unusual
- **Trailing slash**: Spring normalizes — `/users` and `/users/` typically treated the same (configurable)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Class-level @RequestMapping sets the base URL prefix that applies to all methods in the controller. Method-level annotations like @GetMapping or @PostMapping then specify sub-paths relative to that base. Spring concatenates them to form the full URL. This avoids repeating the base path in every method annotation and is also useful for API versioning — you can put the version number in the class-level mapping like /api/v1/users and all methods automatically inherit it. Without a class-level mapping, each method's path is the complete absolute URL from the root. It's a clean organizational pattern that makes controllers easier to read and refactor.

followup_questions: How do you implement API versioning with @RequestMapping?
What happens if both class-level and method-level @RequestMapping define the same path?
Can you map multiple URL paths to the same controller class?

seo.metaTitle: @RequestMapping Class vs Method Level | Spring MVC Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn how class-level and method-level @RequestMapping compose URLs in Spring MVC — base path, URL concatenation, API versioning pattern.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: Class-level @RequestMapping is what keeps your controller methods clean — you declare the base path once, and every method inherits it.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @RequestMapping at the class level sets a base URL prefix for every method in that controller. Method-level @GetMapping and @PostMapping annotations then specify sub-paths relative to that base. Spring concatenates them to form the complete URL.

beats.label: example
beats.content: A class mapped to /api/v1/users with a method mapped to /{id} produces GET /api/v1/users/{id}. Spring handles the slash joining automatically. You don't need to repeat the base in every method.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: This pattern also enables clean API versioning. Put the version number in the class-level path. All methods in that controller automatically include it. When you need a v2, create a new controller class with a v2 base path.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: non-obvious: @RequestMapping can accept an array of paths — both /users and /people can point to the same controller class. This is rarely needed but valid. The same applies at the method level.

speakable_v2.cap: Without a class-level mapping, each method's path is an absolute URL from the root. With one, method paths are relative to it — cleaner and easier to refactor.
